prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: I keep B021 as my preferred configuration, with the same three names. After the full first round I tested it against the chair's question on whether members who regard the pairing mechanism as open can accept a 2026 award. The discovery claimed is a specific, checkable chain: the 2011 continuum-model prediction that interlayer tunnelling flattens the bands near a magic angle, then the 2018 observation of correlated insulating states and superconductivity at that angle. The central observations have been reproduced by many independent groups with transport, scanning tunnelling and capacitance measurements, and the flat-band picture has quantitatively guided later moire work, including topological and fractional Chern states. The mechanism of the superconductivity is a follow-up question, in the same way that the pairing mechanism in the cuprates remained open long after the discovery was recognised. Theory told experimenters where to look and experiment found it, and that tie between calculation and measurement is the one I can judge directly. I have not changed my configuration; round 1 sharpened the weak points but did not change my view of the science.
statement.case_against: Maturity is the real weakness and I do not wish to hide it. The field is eight years old, the pairing mechanism is unsettled, twist-angle disorder makes sample-to-sample details irreproducible, and Danielsson, Olsson and Kroll would prefer to wait. A prize in 2026 would therefore be earlier than for B024 or B020, each with about two decades of independent confirmation. The credit is also incomplete: Cao as first experimental author and the parallel Dean, Yacoby and Young groups cannot be named, and Danielsson's two-name version is a defensible alternative reading. Pearce's question about whether the central discovery will look the same in ten years has a fair answer for the existence of the correlated phases, which I expect to stand, but a less certain one for the interpretation. If the committee judges that the interpretation must be settled first, B024 is the stronger and safer choice.

responses.point: Pearce asks whether the central discovery of B021 will still look the same in ten years and notes that on independent confirmation with understood systematics it is less mature than the clock or neutrino results.
responses.response: I would separate the two things. What I expect to look the same in ten years is the existence of a flat-band regime at a magic angle and the correlated insulating and superconducting phases in it, because transport, tunnelling spectroscopy and compressibility measurements from several groups agree on them, and the flat-band mechanism is already the working design principle for other moire systems. What may change is the interpretation of the pairing, and the citation I propose does not claim to explain it. I accept that the systematics are less tame than in a clock, where the uncertainty budget is a number one can audit, and that this is a legitimate reason to place B024 ahead for a member who weights maturity above all. I would not call it a reason to say that the discovery itself is uncertain.

responses.point: Danielsson would not make B021 the default and would support only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, since Cao cannot be represented and the three-name cut falls on Bistritzer.
responses.response: I still prefer the three-name version, and I want to answer the chair's two-versus-three question directly. The magic-angle prediction is a two-author paper, so a prize naming MacDonald alone for the theory would credit the mechanism to the senior author and leave the junior author who did the calculation off the record. The pair is not wrong as a fallback and I would vote for it before voting against B021, but it fits the 2018 experiment better than the 2011 prediction and the prediction is the half I am most sure of. I agree with you that Cao's role cannot be represented, and this is the main cost of the configuration. I also agree that your B025 is a decisive observation in the plain sense, and I defer to you on astrophysics; my hesitation is only that the optical and redshift credit looks harder to settle in three names than the B021 theory slot.

responses.point: Lindroth prefers B020 because optical lattices give known parameters and quantitative comparison with Monte Carlo and strong-coupling theory, and she worries about sample dependence in twisted bilayer graphene.
responses.response: Your point about quantitative control is right, and it is the clearest scientific advantage of B020 over B021: in a lattice the Hamiltonian is known and in a twisted bilayer it is only approximately known, so sample dependence is a genuine limitation. I would say, though, that the reproducibility I am pointing to in B021 concerns the existence and location of the phases, not their detailed parameters. On your narrowing of B020 to the Mott transition and its proposal, I think that makes the citation tighter, but it also moves it toward the Jaksch-Zoller theory and the Greiner observation of 2002, which is an older discovery that a trio including Bloch, Greiner and Zoller would credit. If the committee goes that way I would regard Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger as the version that matches the simulation programme that was built, and I would rank B020 as my second alternative after the clocks.

responses.point: Kroll argues that optical lattice clocks (B024) are a new measurement capability with clean attribution to Katori and Ye, reproduced at JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB and SYRTE, and says the redefinition of the second rests on it.
responses.response: I agree on reproducibility and on the clean two-name credit, which is a real advantage over the other candidates, and B024 remains my first alternative. Where I still differ is that, as you concede, the outcome so far is tighter limits and an instrument, and the nearest earlier prizes (2005 and 2012) already honoured the comb and ion-control line. I do not regard that as disqualifying and I accept your answer that a capability can itself be the achievement. If the committee as a whole prefers a finished, audited result to a younger discovery of new matter, I would vote for B024 without reservation, and I take your point that a citation anchored on the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 uncertainty separates it from the earlier prizes better than I allowed in round 1.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B021 second and calls it slightly early, and would anchor a B005 citation on the 1995 room-temperature TMR discovery of Moodera and Miyazaki, with the Parkin and Yuasa priority question for MgO still open.
responses.response: Thank you for the clarification on B005. Anchoring on the 1995 discovery is the right way to write it, and it does reduce the attribution problem, but it leaves the citation as a pure Moodera-Miyazaki prize that omits the MgO step that made the effect a device, so I still prefer to keep B005 out of my configuration. On timing, I accept that B021 is slightly early and that this is a risk, not a settled matter. Where I would push back is that waiting would not clearly improve the credit, since the three-name limit will exclude the same experimentalists later. Our difference is about how much confirmation a result needs before the committee acts, not about whether it is real.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a 2026 award in a field whose pairing mechanism is unresolved; if the majority does not, my vote would move to B024.
Whether three names (MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer) or the two-name version is preferable; I favour three but would accept two.
Whether the priority history for B024 (Katori versus Ye and other groups) holds, which I cannot judge from my own subfield.
How the committee weighs a discovery about nature against a new measurement capability; this is a difference of values and not of evidence.
I defer on B025 and B052, which are far from my field, and cannot independently judge the attribution questions there.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict has been identified: I have no recorded connection to MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer or the other shortlisted candidates, and I confirm that no new tie appeared in round 1. My field (DFT, magnetism) is scientifically close to B019, B005 and the theory side of B021, which I treat as proximity and not a conflict.
